blocks.content: You type a domain into your browser. It needs to send a request somewhere, but where exactly, and on whose behalf? The answer reveals two completely different machines that both happen to share the word proxy, and almost nothing else.

A proxy and a reverse proxy are not variations of the same idea. They solve opposite problems, sit on opposite sides of a connection, and protect opposite parties. This topic covers what each one actually does, the real tools behind them, where the two get genuinely confused, and how to reason about either one cleanly in a system design interview.
1. The One-Line Difference
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273895948-304833964.png
blocks.alt: The single question that instantly tells you which kind of proxy you are looking at

blocks.content: A forward proxy hides the client from the server it is talking to. A reverse proxy hides the servers from the client making the request. Same word, opposite sides, opposite jobs, and almost everything else about tools, configuration, and use cases follows directly from that one distinction.

Every remaining section in this topic is, in a real sense, just an elaboration of this one sentence, once the direction of hiding is settled, the rest is simply which specific problem that direction happens to be useful for solving.
2. What Is a Forward Proxy
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273898169-433791544.png
blocks.alt: The client is explicitly configured to use the proxy, and the destination server only ever sees the proxy, never the real client

blocks.content: A forward proxy sits between a client and the internet, and the client knows about it, it is explicitly configured to send its traffic there. When the client wants to reach any destination, the request goes to the proxy first, the proxy forwards it onward, and the destination server's response comes back through the same path. The destination server never sees the original client at all, only the proxy.

This is the exact configuration a corporate network or a VPN client sets up deliberately, the client's own network settings are changed to point every outbound request at the proxy first, rather than reaching the destination directly.
3. What Forward Proxies Actually Do
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273900013-747088268.png
blocks.alt: A forward proxy exists to control, hide, or optimize outbound traffic on the client's own side of the connection

blocks.content: Every outbound request flowing through one choke point makes content filtering possible, entire categories of sites can be blocked outright, exactly what schools and corporations rely on heavily. Since the destination only sees the proxy's own IP, not the real client's, this is also the foundation of anonymity tools and VPNs, a VPN connection routes your traffic through a forward proxy, making every website believe you are wherever that proxy physically sits.

If hundreds of employees all load the same news homepage each morning, the proxy can fetch it once and serve the cached copy to everyone else, zero additional internet requests for the other users. A proxy located in a specific country also makes requests appear to originate from there, letting a service decide what content to show based on the proxy's location rather than the client's real one. And because every request passes through it, a forward proxy naturally produces a complete log of everything every user did, exactly what compliance requirements in finance and healthcare often mandate.

blocks.title: Real Tools
blocks.content: Squid, Nginx configured in forward mode, corporate VPN gateways, and Tor, which is essentially a multi-hop forward proxy, are all real, common implementations of this exact pattern.
4. What Is a Reverse Proxy
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273901638-167644141.png
blocks.alt: The client has no idea the reverse proxy exists at all, it believes it is talking directly to the website

blocks.content: A reverse proxy sits between the internet and your own servers. Clients have no idea it exists, they believe they are talking directly to the application. The reverse proxy receives every incoming request, and your actual backend servers live on a private network, entirely unreachable from the public internet on their own, the reverse proxy is the only public-facing component, your infrastructure's actual front door.

This is precisely the opposite orientation from a forward proxy, there the client explicitly opted in and the server was the one kept in the dark, here the server side deliberately hides its own internal structure while the client remains entirely unaware anything sits in between at all.
5. What Reverse Proxies Actually Do
A reverse proxy distributes incoming requests across a pool of backend servers so no single one drowns under the full load.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273903334-763085644.png
blocks.alt: Different algorithms spread load differently, and the right one depends on what the backends actually need

blocks.content: Round robin distributes requests evenly in sequence. Least connections routes each new request to whichever backend currently has the fewest active connections. IP hash sends the same client consistently to the same backend, useful when a backend still holds some session state locally.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027097-922600773.png
blocks.alt: A crashed backend is detected within seconds, and traffic simply stops flowing to it, invisibly to every user

blocks.content: If a backend goes down, the proxy's own health checker notices within seconds and stops routing to it entirely, users never see a failed request at all, traffic simply flows to the remaining healthy servers instead.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273906596-703681855.png
blocks.alt: The reverse proxy holds the certificate and handles encryption, so backend servers only ever need to speak plain HTTP internally

blocks.content: Backends can run plain HTTP internally while the reverse proxy alone holds the TLS certificate, performs the HTTPS handshake with the client, decrypts the traffic, and forwards plain HTTP inward. This means exactly one certificate to manage and renew, simpler backend configuration, and the CPU cost of TLS encryption offloaded from every application server onto one dedicated, optimized component.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273908354-978155973.png
blocks.alt: A cached response is served directly from the proxy, without the request ever reaching the backend or its database at all

blocks.content: The proxy can cache backend responses and serve them directly for identical subsequent requests. A product page taking eighty milliseconds to generate from a database can be cached so that, for the next minute, every request for it is served in under a millisecond directly from the proxy's own memory, the database never queried again for that page at all.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273909902-833894802.png
blocks.alt: The reverse proxy is the first thing attack traffic hits, and it can absorb and filter most of it before the real origin ever sees a single request

blocks.content: The reverse proxy is the very first thing malicious traffic reaches, letting it identify and drop harmful patterns, IP blocklists, per-client rate limits, before any of it ever reaches the actual application at all.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273911724-26146074.png
blocks.alt: One public domain can quietly front several completely independent backend services, routed purely by URL path

blocks.content: A reverse proxy can inspect the URL path of an incoming request and route it to entirely different backend services, one domain in front of many independent services, each deployable and scalable completely on its own, with clients never noticing the difference.

blocks.title: Real Tools
blocks.content: Nginx, HAProxy, Cloudflare, AWS Application Load Balancer, Traefik, and Caddy are all genuine, widely used reverse proxy implementations.
6. Forward vs Reverse at a Glance

7. Real-World Examples

blocks.title: A Corporate Forward Proxy
blocks.text: A company requires all internet traffic to route through a head office proxy first. An employee's browser is configured to send every request there. Opening a blocked site returns a policy notice instantly, the request never leaves the building. Opening an allowed site gets logged, checked against cache, and forwarded, the destination sees only the proxy's IP, never the employee's laptop directly.

blocks.title: A Reverse Proxy in Front of Three Backends
blocks.text: A team runs the same application on three separate servers, with nginx sitting in front on port 443 holding the TLS certificate. Every user believes they are talking directly to the site, nginx terminates HTTPS, forwards plain HTTP to whichever backend currently has the fewest active connections, and if one backend crashes, the health check detects it within seconds and quietly routes everyone else's traffic to the two that remain healthy.

blocks.title: Reverse Proxying at Massive Scale
blocks.text: A domain's DNS points directly at a global edge network with hundreds of points of presence worldwide. Every request is scrubbed for DDoS traffic, rate limited, checked for bot behavior, cached, and TLS-terminated before a single request ever reaches the real origin server, which itself might be one modest instance, made to look like a fortress purely by what sits in front of it.

blocks.content: 8. Where It Gets Subtle
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273913296-860288031.png
blocks.alt: A load balancer is only one of several things a full reverse proxy typically does

blocks.content: A load balancer is one of the things a reverse proxy can do, but a reverse proxy usually does considerably more. A pure load balancer only distributes traffic, a reverse proxy also commonly handles TLS termination, caching, path-based routing, authentication, and security, which is exactly why tools like Nginx and HAProxy that do both get the two terms used almost interchangeably in casual conversation.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273914953-834812767.png
blocks.alt: Nothing prevents the exact same organization from running both kinds of proxy at once, for entirely different purposes

blocks.content: A single organization can genuinely run both at once. A corporate proxy filtering outbound employee traffic is a forward proxy, while that same company's own internal tools might sit behind a completely separate reverse proxy. The direction of what is being hidden is what matters, not which specific software happens to be installed, the exact same tool, Nginx, can be configured as either one depending purely on its configuration.
9. X-Forwarded-For: Recovering the Real Client IP
blocks.text: 9. X-Forwarded-For: Recovering the Real Client IP

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273916516-286983639.png
blocks.alt: Without an explicit header, a backend behind a reverse proxy only ever sees the proxy's own IP, never the real client's

blocks.content: When a reverse proxy forwards a request to a backend, the backend sees the proxy's own IP as the apparent source, not the real client's. To fix this, the proxy adds an X-Forwarded-For header carrying the genuine client IP, and the backend reads that header whenever it actually needs to know who made the request.

Without this header, every single line in your backend's own logs would show the reverse proxy's IP, and only the reverse proxy's IP, for every request from every user, making it impossible to distinguish one real client from another after the fact.

The example below simulates exactly the two load balancing algorithms covered earlier, choosing a backend through round robin across six requests, then choosing backends through least connections given three backends with different starting connection counts, showing precisely which backend each new request actually lands on.
10. Transparent Proxies
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027284-334852360.png
blocks.alt: A transparent proxy intercepts traffic without the client ever being configured to use it at all

blocks.content: Every forward proxy covered so far required the client to be explicitly configured to use it. A transparent proxy skips that requirement entirely, the network itself silently redirects traffic through the proxy, and the client never even knows a proxy is involved. Internet service providers and corporate networks sometimes deploy these specifically so that outbound filtering or logging works even for devices no one bothered to configure individually.
11. Open Proxies: A Real Security Risk
blocks.text: 11. Open Proxies: A Real Security Risk

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027098-53987991.png
blocks.alt: A proxy that accepts requests from absolutely anyone becomes a tool an attacker can freely route traffic through

blocks.content: A misconfigured proxy, forward or reverse, that accepts connections from anyone on the internet rather than only its intended users is called an open proxy. Attackers actively scan for these specifically to route malicious traffic through them, hiding their own origin behind someone else's infrastructure entirely. Restricting exactly who is allowed to use a proxy is not an optional hardening step, it is a basic requirement for operating one safely at all.
12. Sidecar Proxies in Modern Microservices
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273922004-78549275.png
blocks.alt: In a service mesh, every individual service gets its own dedicated proxy instance rather than sharing one central one

blocks.content: Modern microservice architectures often push the reverse proxy pattern down to the level of a single service. A sidecar proxy, tools like Envoy are common here, runs alongside every individual service instance, handling that one service's own TLS, retries, and traffic routing, rather than every service sharing one large, central reverse proxy. This is the foundation of what is commonly called a service mesh, applying the exact same reverse proxy ideas covered throughout this topic, just at a much finer, per-service grain.
13. How This Fits Into a System Design Interview
blocks.text: 13. How This Fits Into a System Design Interview

blocks.content: As soon as a design draws clients hitting servers directly, adding a reverse proxy in between is worth mentioning explicitly, framed as the single entry point handling TLS termination, load balancing across the backend fleet, and a natural place to add DDoS protection later. If the design involves several independent services, auth, payments, search, the reverse proxy is exactly how they get exposed under one public domain without clients ever needing to know which internal port each one actually runs on.

Mentioning that backends run plain HTTP internally while the proxy alone holds the certificate shows a clear understanding of where cryptographic work should actually live. For load balancing choice, round robin or least connections usually fits stateless APIs well, while IP hash or, better still, making sessions themselves stateless through something like signed tokens, avoids relying on sticky sessions at all. A forward proxy is worth raising specifically when the design involves internal employees accessing tools, compliance requirements around outbound logging, or controlling exactly what external services an internal system is allowed to reach.
14. The One-Line Test
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785273923653-862974288.png
blocks.alt: One question resolves any ambiguity about which kind of proxy you are actually looking at

blocks.content: Faced with an unfamiliar proxy, ask exactly one question: who is being hidden? If the client is hidden from the server, it is a forward proxy. If the servers are hidden from the client, it is a reverse proxy. Everything else, the specific tools, the exact use cases, the configuration details, follows directly from that single answer.
15. A Common Mistake: Forgetting X-Forwarded-For
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027096-322762786.png
blocks.alt: Every single backend log entry silently shows the same proxy IP for every distinct user, unless the header is explicitly read

blocks.content: A recurring, easy to miss mistake is deploying a reverse proxy and never configuring the backend to actually read the X-Forwarded-For header. Every log entry then shows the exact same proxy IP for every single request, from every different user, making it impossible to distinguish genuine traffic patterns, investigate abuse, or apply any per-client rate limiting at the application layer at all.
Worked Example

A growing company starts with a single Node.js server directly exposed to the internet. As traffic grows, they add nginx in front, holding the TLS certificate and load balancing across three application servers using least connections. Six months later, they split their monolith into separate auth, payments, and search services, and extend that same nginx configuration to route by URL path, one domain, three independent backends, with no client ever noticing the internal restructuring.

Separately, that same company's internal engineering tools sit behind their own forward proxy, every employee's outbound traffic to external services is logged for a compliance requirement tied to handling financial data, entirely independent of the customer-facing reverse proxy described above.

Years later, as the same company adopts a full microservices architecture with dozens of independently deployed services, they migrate from one shared reverse proxy toward a sidecar proxy running alongside every individual service instance, the same underlying idea, just applied at a much finer grain to match the new architecture's own shape.

blocks.content: Practice

Sketch a small company's network: employees behind a forward proxy for compliance logging, and that same company's customer-facing product behind a reverse proxy handling TLS and load balancing across three backends. Label clearly, on each side of each proxy, exactly who is hidden from whom.
Then design a path-based routing scheme for a single domain fronting four independent services, auth, payments, search, and notifications, deciding the exact URL path prefix each one should own.

Finally, walk through the exact request path a payment request follows from the client through the reverse proxy to a backend, and identify precisely which header the backend needs to check to recover the real client IP for its own fraud detection logic.
Key Takeaway

A forward proxy hides the client from the server, sitting on the client's own side of a connection, used for content filtering, anonymity, and compliance logging. A reverse proxy hides the servers from the client, sitting in front of your own infrastructure, used for load balancing, TLS termination, caching, and DDoS protection. The one question that resolves any confusion between them is simply who is being hidden, and everything else about tools, configuration, and use cases follows directly from that single answer.
